thesis: Reframing why this is held, because the original reason no longer applies. TLT has returned +0.43% over a month while SPY fell 4.96% — outperformance of 5.39% — so it is doing real work as the only hedge against fifteen equity longs. It is not working because rates are falling: the Fed is ~95% priced to hike on Dec 9.
key_risk: Tomorrow's 08:30 ET core PCE is consensus 3.2% y/y against 3.1% prior. A hot print strengthens the hiking path, and with the 10y at 4.92% and a second January hike ~57% priced, the 84.3 target sits above the 84.34 90-day high and is not consistent with that rate path. The honest expectation is that this position hedges rather than reaches its target.
counter_argument: The strongest case against holding: buying 20-year duration two weeks before a near-certain hike, with inflation re-accelerating, is fighting the stated regime. If the equity book is the thing that needs hedging, cash or short-duration does it without the duration risk — and if PCE runs hot, TLT and the equity longs can fall together, which is exactly what did NOT happen on 11/20 and is the scenario that breaks the hedge.

catalyst.action: CLOSE the existing DKS long (opened 2026-11-13 at 144.5). This is an EXIT of a held position, not a new short — sell the shares, do not establish a short. Exit into the 131.0-136.4 band. Re-entry is a separate trade: only inside or below the 128.70-136.39 insider band and only with its own stop below the 120.15 ninety-day low.

thesis: Closing a position whose entry price, not whose thesis, is wrong. From spot 133.67 the target at 175.5 is 31.3% away while the 129.0 stop is 3.5% away — 0.70 ATR on a 4.96% ATR name — so the odds of the target printing first are roughly 10-15% against a 33% break-even. Exiting near 133 instead of at 129 is the whole edge here, and it is worth about 3.5%.
key_risk: DKS is the best-evidenced long in the book at the wrong price, so this exit can look foolish within days: seven insiders bought between 128.70 and 136.39 and 11/23 put through the heaviest volume of the window on an up day. If the insider band holds as support, closing here sells the bottom. The win_probability of 0.85 is the chance the exit beats holding to the stop, not a directional forecast — read it that way.
counter_argument: The strongest case against closing: a seven-person, $5.59M insider cluster bracketing the current price is the single most predictive public signal available, and the position is only 7.5% underwater with a defined 3.5% of remaining risk. Holding risks 3.5% to keep exposure to that cluster. The reason it still loses: the published 175.5 target is unreachable in a swing horizon and every repair route fails a floor, so holding is paying 3.5% for a trade that cannot reach its own target.

evidence.detail: Fetched OHLCV: spot 133.67 vs stop 129.0 is 0.70x the 6.63 ATR, while the 175.5 target is 31.3% above spot; sma20 142.48 sits BELOW the 144.5 entry, so no reachable target yields positive reward from entry. 90d range 120.151-220.36, i.e. -39.34% off the high

thesis: The best-structured equity-side position in the book and the only one with two independent drivers pulling in opposite directions, which is why it has gone nowhere in 21 days. The bond-proxy leg is a headwind into a hiking Fed; the datacenter power-demand leg was just handed new life, since Nvidia's AI capex cycle is what drives utility load growth and that trade restarted on 11/23.
key_risk: Utilities are the cleanest bond proxy in the sector lineup and the Fed is ~95% priced to hike on Dec 9 with a second January hike ~57% priced. If tomorrow's core PCE prints hot, the rate leg overwhelms the power-demand leg and the 41.8 stop comes into play. The position has also produced exactly 0.0% in 21 days, so it is consuming capital for no return.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: holding a bond proxy into a hiking cycle is the same error that explains this book's 11% hit rate, and the power-demand story is a multi-year thesis being used to justify a swing position with a 3.5% stop. The answer is structural, not narrative — XLU is one of only two positions in the book trading above its 50-day, and its 1.51% ATR is the lowest of any open position, so it is the cheapest place in the book to be wrong.
